`apa_reliability` reports useful aspects of a reliability analysis. For each item, it shows:

* the mean (*M*) and standard deviation (*SD*), which reveal ceiling and floor effects
* the corrected item–total correlation (*r*~it~), the item's correlation with the sum of the *other* items in its scale. Items with low values (often, below .30) discriminate poorly.
* Cronbach's α if the item were deleted. A value above the scale's α means that the item lowers reliability.

Below each scale's items are its scale-level statistics: the mean and *SD* of the scale scores, Cronbach's α with a confidence interval, McDonald's *ω*~total~, and the mean inter-item correlation. Cronbach's α [@cronbachCoefficientAlphaInternal1951] assumes that all items are equally good measures of what the scale measures, while *ω*~total~ allows them to differ, so many journals now ask for both. The mean inter-item correlation shows whether a high α comes from strongly related items or merely from many items.

The statistics come from the [psych](https://personality-project.org/r/psych/) package: `psych::alpha` for α and the item statistics, and a one-factor model (`psych::fa`) for *ω*~total~. The confidence interval of α is Feldt's.

# Several Scales

The `bfi` data set in the psychTools package [@revellePsychToolsToolsAccompany2019] has the answers of 2,800 people to 25 personality items, on a scale from 1 (*very inaccurate*) to 6 (*very accurate*). The items are named by codes (A1 to A5 for agreeableness, and so on), and `bfi.dictionary` has their wording. The table is easier to read with the wording, so rename the items with it, and keep a lookup vector from codes to wording for choosing the items of each scale:

```{r}
#| label: data
items <- psychTools::bfi.dictionary[1:25, ]
# Item wording without the final period, named by item code
item_text <- setNames(sub("[.]$", "", items$Item), rownames(items))

d_bfi <- psychTools::bfi[, names(item_text)]
names(d_bfi) <- item_text
```

Give `apa_reliability` a named list of scales, each a vector of item names. Items worded in the opposite direction (e.g., "Am indifferent to the feelings of others" on the agreeableness scale) are reverse-scored with `reverse`. `item_range` gives the lowest and highest possible responses, which are used to reverse the items:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bfi-reliability
#| tbl-cap: "Item Analysis of the Agreeableness and Conscientiousness Scales"
bfi_scales <- list(
  Agreeableness = item_text[paste0("A", 1:5)],
  Conscientiousness = item_text[paste0("C", 1:5)]
)
bfi_reverse <- item_text[c("A1", "C4", "C5")]

apa_reliability(
  d_bfi,
  scales = bfi_scales,
  reverse = bfi_reverse,
  item_range = c(1, 6)
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Each scale has a heading, with its items and statistics indented below it. Reverse-scored items are marked (R). Each scale uses the respondents who answered all of its items, and the note gives their number.

"Am indifferent to the feelings of others" has the weakest item–total correlation of the agreeableness items (.31), and deleting it would raise α slightly, from .70 to .72. With `flag = .30`, item–total correlations below .30 and values of α if deleted that exceed the scale's α are bolded:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bfi-flag
#| tbl-cap: "Item Analysis With Flagged Items"
apa_reliability(
  d_bfi,
  scales = bfi_scales,
  reverse = bfi_reverse,
  item_range = c(1, 6),
  flag = .30
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

# One Row per Scale

When the items have been examined and the paper reports only the scales, `level = "scales"` gives one row per scale. This table pairs naturally with a correlation table of the scale scores (see `apa_cor`).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bfi-scales
#| tbl-cap: "Reliability of the Big Five Scales"
apa_reliability(
  d_bfi,
  scales = list(
    Agreeableness = item_text[paste0("A", 1:5)],
    Conscientiousness = item_text[paste0("C", 1:5)],
    Extraversion = item_text[paste0("E", 1:5)],
    Neuroticism = item_text[paste0("N", 1:5)],
    Openness = item_text[paste0("O", 1:5)]
  ),
  reverse = item_text[c("A1", "C4", "C5", "E1", "E2", "O2", "O5")],
  item_range = c(1, 6),
  level = "scales"
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

# Test Items Scored 0 or 1

For tests whose items are scored correct (1) or incorrect (0), *M* is the item's difficulty (the proportion of correct answers), *r*~it~ is the corrected point-biserial correlation, and α equals the Kuder–Richardson formula 20 [KR-20\; @kuderTheoryEstimationTest1937]. `apa_reliability` detects such items and says so in the table and the note. Here, 300 simulated students answered 6 items of increasing difficulty:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-binary
#| tbl-cap: "Item Analysis of Six Simulated Binary Test Items"
set.seed(1)
ability <- rnorm(300)
difficulty <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 6)
test_items <- sapply(difficulty, \(b) rbinom(300, 1, plogis(ability - b)))
colnames(test_items) <- paste("Item", 1:6)

apa_reliability(as.data.frame(test_items)) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

With a single scale, there is no scale heading. Six items of modest discrimination give a low KR-20; longer tests are usually needed for dependable scores.

# Options

* `omega = FALSE` leaves out *ω*~total~.
* `score = "sum"` reports the mean and *SD* of the scale sums instead of the scale means.
* `ci` sets the confidence level of the interval of α (e.g., `ci = .90`).
* `format_variable_names = FALSE` keeps item and scale names exactly as they are.
